title: Precision in Word and Image
use_cases: Use when selecting vocabulary based on emotional and cultural context rather than dictionary definition
Implement when replacing general adjectives like 'angry' or 'sad' with precise physical actions
Configure when drafting descriptive passages to move from abstract generalities to concrete imagery
Use when evaluating metaphors to ensure they are original and thematic rather than cliché
Implement when transforming flat prose into immersive storytelling through sensory descriptions
content:
Every word is a choice. To elevate your prose, you must choose words not just for their dictionary definition (denotation) but for their emotional and cultural baggage (connotation). A “house” is a structure. A “home” is a feeling. A “residence” is a legal status. All refer to the same thing, but each word paints a vastly different picture.

Strive for specificity. Instead of saying a character is “angry,” show it through precise action and sensory detail. Did their knuckles turn white? Did a vein pulse in their temple? Did their voice drop to a low, dangerous hum? Generalities tell; specifics show and immerse.

| General | Specific |
| --- | --- |
| The car drove fast. | The Mustang tore down the asphalt. |
| It was a nice day. | The sun was warm on the skin, a gentle breeze rustling the new leaves. |
| She was sad. | A single tear traced a path through the dust on her cheek. |

This principle extends to figurative language. Clichéd metaphors and similes flatten prose. “Her eyes were like the sea” is tired. What kind of sea? A calm, turquoise Mediterranean? A churning, grey North Atlantic? Or are they like the sea after a storm, littered with wreckage? Original, vivid imagery that connects to the story’s themes will always have more power.
